- Screening qualified eight items, all of them on resource assignment (the resource family expected about 0.01 items by chance); no control-flow or timing difference passed the thresholds. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]

- On six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22) the resources doing the work changed markedly. In the earlier window, one resource (User_32) held the largest share of each — roughly 11–13% on five of them and 16% on A22 — with a handful of others at about 3–8%. In the later window, User_32 and its companions drop out of the top ranks, and a different set of about ten resources shares the work at roughly 4–11% each (User_46 tops A22 at about 11%); a few of the rising resources already appear earlier with smaller shares. Cosine dissimilarity is 0.40–0.66, each difference larger than in all but about one of 2,000 random re-splits, and each profile rests on roughly 110–260 observations per window. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

- A07 changed most sharply: earlier its work was spread across 14 distinct resources with the largest holding about 23% (concentration index 0.11); in the later window a single resource (User_52) handled every observed execution (top share 100%, concentration index 1.0), based on 84 and 90 observations. [ASSIGN003, CONC001]

- The same two groups recur across activities: the resources losing share overlap strongly from activity to activity, as do the resources gaining share, while the residual "other" bucket stays at roughly 35–52% of assignments in both windows — the shift concerns the visible top of the allocation, not its diffuse tail. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that resource allocation changed: in the later window, work on A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 moved from the group of resources that previously carried the largest shares (led by User_32) to a largely different group of resources, and A07 — previously shared across 14 resources — was handled by a single resource (User_52) in every observed case. This rests on direct assignment profiles for each activity, a screening yield far above chance (eight resource items where about 0.01 were expected), differences larger than in essentially all of 2,000 random re-splits, the same before- and after-groups recurring across activities, and the concentration measure independently confirming the A07 collapse from 14 resources to one. Limitations: the profiles show only the top ten resources plus a residual bucket still holding roughly 35–52% of assignments, so continued small involvement of the earlier group cannot be excluded, and A13/A14 have identical profiles and likely reflect one underlying behaviour rather than two. An important competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is a shift in the mix of cases (case types that the earlier group used to handle becoming more common) rather than an explicit reassignment; no control-flow or timing items qualified that could tie the allocation shift to a change in case paths. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]
